utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the registrar to call out the case number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances, please? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson and Mr. Waespi for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Toma Fila here with Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Kosic lives quite some distance away, so he hasn't been able to reach us in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dokmanovic, good morning. Can you hear me? Thank you. Let me start by thanking, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, both parties for promptly accepting our suggestions to bring forward the resumption of our trial. We are really most obliged and very appreciative of the cooperative attitude of both parties. As you know, this will enable us to finish another trial next Monday when we will be sitting on a different case, and then we will resume on Tuesday, as you know. Now, before we start, let me deal with a few housekeeping matters. First of all, I hope that Mr. Fila has seen the urgent request for assistance to the Republic of Croatia which I immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And I wish to thank you for it. I really thank you very much because it worked because my investigator was able to go to Vukovar yesterday, so I thank the court for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. It's very good news because I was prepared even to phone the Ambassador of Croatia to The Hague, but I see there is no point now. Excellent. So this proves that the Croatian authorities are cooperating very well. Then I would like again to ask the parties about the various witnesses they would like to call today. I understand Mr. Fila is calling five witnesses this morning, probably, or today, five witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I will call four witnesses this morning, but the fifth witness is waiting in the hotel, so if we finish on time, we can also hear him. Not a problem at all. At any rate, I will finish today, maybe not in the morning but for sure in the afternoon. It doesn't depend on me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you are also calling today the expert witness, Professor Aleksic. We have received the English translation of his statement. Very good. Now, I am not clear about the list of three witnesses for whom you have enclosed in your document, the document filed recently, the written statements. These are Dragisic Mirko, Novakovic, and Tomasevic. I think we heard those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, but these are not the same statements. This is what this is all about. Since we are talking now informally, since I heard that the tape is being disputed, I heard about that from Mr. Williamson on the 28th, 29th, and then I read the statement by Mr. Dzuro, I asked them to provide me with their copies of the tape, that's what I asked of Mr. Dragisic and Tomasevic, because they also got the tapes in 1991, and they provided me with those tapes. The statements tell you that under oath they stated that they gave me those tapes, and I am prepared to give you those tapes whenever you feel like it. It's the same tape as the master tapes, and these are just the copies of the tape that you already have as D2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but you are not going to call again those two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. No. Not a single one of them. There has been a misunderstanding. Mr. Vasic will testify as to their statements. This will be in rebuttal of the evidence provided by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said the master tape. Did you mean to refer to the original copy of the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. The first copy is the copy that you have, and the expert of the Prosecutor, as I can see, also stated that. But from that tape, those two copies were made, and those copies were given to those two witnesses, but that was in 1991. For us, it is important to determine that these tapes were shot in 1991 in their present form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning now to the Prosecution. I understand they are going to call eight witnesses, and some of them are expert witnesses; namely, Dr. Tabbush, Mr. Herold, Professor Wagenaar, and Dr. Gudjonsson; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when do you intend to call those witnesses? This week or next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's anticipated, Your Honours, that the order that we have to call witnesses will be as follows: We will call the investigator, Mr. Vladimir Dzuro, either today or tomorrow, we will call the expert witness on the trees, Mr. Tabbush, tomorrow, and then we will call Witness R, we have sought protection for him, tomorrow as well, and then next week it's anticipated that we will call Mr. Herold, Witness S, and Mr. Corwin, and then, finally, Dr. Wagenaar. Finally, yes, Dr. Gudjonsson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Concerning the expert witnesses, you may have noticed that the Defence counsel raised a few issues in particular concerning the CVs, and I think I agree with Mr. Fila that, if possible, CVs should be handed both to Defence counsel and to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, I don't know whether you have noticed, but yesterday we filed a response to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In that motion, we provided the CVs. Mr. Fila has also raised the issue of wanting our letters to the experts, which we're not prepared to provide. It's work product. What we are prepared to provide is the questions we asked the experts and asked them to opine on, and we have done that in our response, which Mr. Fila presumably should have or, in due course, will be served with if he hasn't got it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did receive it, yes. I received the response, I received the CVs, not on the 12th or on the 15th, but yesterday. I just wanted to turn your attention to the fact that I stick to the deadlines that you issue in your orders, and I again received these too late because on the 15th I was supposed to give my response. The reason why I asked for the letter is because they gave answers with regard to that letter, so I could have been given the letter because it just shows what was written to those two experts, Wagenaar and Gudjonsson. I can't force them, of course, to give me that, but I think that the court maybe can force them to give me that because I don't know what the questions were, yet I received their answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, he certainly has the questions now, and we're in a similar position with respect to the information about his Professor Aleksic. We didn't receive any CVs or any of his report until now either, so we're in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And he's calling Dr. Aleksic today. We just received the CVs, Your Honours. We provided the reports last week in compliance with the order, so any suggestion there hasn't been compliance with the order is rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no. Your Honour, I submitted everything on time. I was not allowed to provide my own translations in accordance with the registry decision. I don't know how many times I have to repeat that. I submit it as soon as I get it, and I don't know how long it takes for the translation to be done. I wanted to do the translations myself, but I wasn't allowed to do so, so it's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, we certainly didn't receive it, Your Honour. We received it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What? The CV?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, the report. We still haven't received the CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, sorry, the CV of Professor Aleksic was next to the document filed on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, the report. We just received it this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The report, yes, but I agree with Mr. Fila, I must say, this is because of the amount of work of the translation unit. It was handed in in Serbo Croatian and then it was translated -- actually, it's a draft translation, I read here, by the translation unit in the Tribunal, who are, of course, overwhelmed with requests for translation. But I would not enter into any polemics because I think, by and large, both parties are cooperating, and we do appreciate the problems you may face in some instances. So the only issue which is probably worth discussing is whether or not the Prosecutor should provide both the Defence counsel and the court with the text of their own requests or letters to Professor Wagenaar and Gudjonsson. However, since, of course, we cannot but trust the Prosecutor, if the Prosecutor is ready to give us the list of questions they actually put to both experts, I think we should be happy with that. As long as we know what questions were put to both experts, we can understand the whole set of issues much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The questions are fairly straightforward, Your Honours, and it's not a complex issue. This is rebuttal evidence, so it's obviously not going to be expansive, the information we sought, and as I say, we have provided in our response. But I think this touches on a very germane question in relation to the issue of discovery and responsibilities. I mean, the parties do have a necessity to investigate and to obtain information, and it may be that the information is unhelpful or unnecessary, so there is an exploration process that goes on both by the Defence and by the Prosecution. It would be oppressive to request the Defence to provide work product material in relation to their correspondence with witnesses. In some jurisdictions, this is covered by legal professional privilege; in others, it is covered as work product. Your Honours, in my submission, certainly it assists all parties for them to know what was asked. But it's not as though these witnesses are just some sort of statement tendered in a vacuum; they're going to be called. Mr. Fila is quite at liberty to get up and ask questions. If the professor or the doctor has the information at hand, he can respond. He can say what was the nature of correspondence between the parties. The whole process of cross-examination is designed to permit this to happen, and it doesn't necessitate delving into speculative issues which could arise as a consequence of the investigative process, whereby large amounts of material are rejected. That just becomes especially true when it relates to a rebuttal case because in a rebuttal case you are confining it to a very, very narrow concept. You may ask a wider, broader range of questions, but when it comes to the actual testimony of the witness, you want to concentrate on what truly represents rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We do agree with the Prosecution, and I think we will be content with the list of questions that I understand have already been submitted to the court and the Defence counsel. We have not yet received this document which probably was filed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I'm happy to see that Mr. Fila has got it. Now, let us now therefore move on and start with the witnesses, if there are no other matters, with the witnesses called by the -- yes, Mr. Fila, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You may have noticed, Your Honours, I also said something else in my motion. In the system in which I have been acting as a Defence counsel for 30 years -- it's a long time, but that's how it is -- the behaviour of the person on trial is important up to the time when he is acquitted or convicted; even after that, in the sentencing proceedings. I propose that the court should obtain the information about the behaviour of Mr. Dokmanovic from the moment of his arrest up until his trial. That means the medical records from the prison or maybe even testimony by Mr. McFadden, the warden of the prison. That's the system in my country. So this is just my proposal. This is not something that I request. Because we have had secondhand evidence, expert witness, Vera Petrovic, said that she had seen the medical records of Mr. Dokmanovic and saw what was written in there, but you haven't seen this medical record. So if the Trial Chamber deems that this is necessary, I just wanted to make that suggestion. I can see that the Prosecutor is not opposed that this medical record be examined by Your Honours and maybe even Mr. McFadden may testify here or submit a written report on the behaviour of Mr. Dokmanovic, on the conduct of Mr. Dokmanovic. This is just an explanation of my motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, you could assist the court by clarifying for what purposes you are proposing that medical records should be looked at by the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because in my country, in the sentencing proceedings, the fact whether a person has a previous criminal record, the fact of his conduct, aggressive conduct in prison, or his health situation, if he refuses to obey the orders of the guards and so on or if he behaves in a different manner, this is something that's important. This is the reason why I propose this. If you deem it necessary, okay; if not, okay again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You know, this is a delicate matter because this is an issue which may give rise to a question of intrusion into the privacy of medical records, medical data, things which we --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: With the approval, with his approval and the approval of his Defence, I hereby give you our consent that his medical record be examined, just as we gave our consent for Mrs. Petrovic to examine this record. Otherwise, she wouldn't have been able to examine the record at all. But again, I stress, if the court deems it necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution whether they have any views on this particular matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, except that it may assist the court more if Mr. Fila was to perhaps seek the court's assistance in securing this evidence to be brought before the court if he considers it to be relevant and would assist in the sentencing process. It may just be a little awkward otherwise in terms of leading the evidence from the witness and being responsible for discussing the issue with the witnesses that he wants to call. It seems to me that Your Honours may be better assisted if Mr. Fila is responsible for these witnesses and perhaps seeks Your Honours' assistance in securing their attendance. One of them is a United Nations witness and is not amenable to examination without special exemption, I understand, so that needs to be obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This would be -- are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. McFadden, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: McFadden.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand the situation to be that way, but I wouldn't like to speak, but I think there is some restriction on U.N. personnel testifying. But that can be overcome and, of course, it just means that steps need to be taken to secure the approval, I think, of New York, is the process that one obtains. But it's a little awkward for Your Honours to take it upon yourselves to handle witnesses and bring them before the court. You can do it. There is provisions in the Rules for it. No one says it can't happen. But it may be better if that responsibility is left with Mr. Fila, with Your Honours' assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The court feels that the best solution would be as follows: We will ask the medical officer in charge of the prison -- I don't remember his name -- to produce a medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Falces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dr. Falces, yes, Dr. Falces, to submit a detailed medical report, in a language which is accessible to people who are not experts in medicine, on the physical medical conditions of the accused. So that we would simply receive this medical -- the court will request -- it's not for Mr. Fila -- the court will request the medical officer of the prison to produce this medical report. I wonder whether Mr. Fila, as I think I understood him to say, also wants to have some sort of report on the behaviour of the accused while in prison. We could ask Mr. McFadden again to submit a report on the behaviour of the accused while in detention. So we would have two written statements from the two relevant offices. May I take this opportunity, since we are talking about evidence which is relevant to the sentencing, may I turn to the Prosecution and ask them to clarify whether two of their witnesses, namely, these are U.N. civil servants, I think, Mr. Corwin and Witness S, who are going to report or testify on the attitude of the accused in a period subsequent to the relevant date, I mean, the crucial date, '91; namely, the period '93-'94 or '94-'95, whether this evidence is relevant in the view of the Prosecution again for sentencing purposes, because otherwise it would not be material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. Is Your Honour directing your question to the fact of it being subsequent or is Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. Yes. Your Honours, in our submission, evidence of attitudes and views on certain events is relevant subsequently if it's the views held by a person and, in our submission, is admissible. So it's not, when talking of general character evidence and on questions of sentencing, it's not excluded merely because it's subsequent. There are bases upon which subsequent conduct are admissible. It's not always admissible, but it can be depending upon the character of the evidence itself, such as views held, if a person holds a particular political belief or a particular religious belief or whatever, an attitude to a certain thing. Those are views that can be held for a lifetime, and someone can come along at a point and give evidence of that. This evidence won't be evidence in a vacuum because there will be other evidence from another witness about similar views held prior to the event, so it will, in effect, show a link, continuity between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So that is how it will become admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's not only relevant for sentencing purposes but to cover the whole period. I mean, the attitude both before '91, or in '91 and after '91.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I will say that it was a continuation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It shows presumably, you would say, a consistency --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Niemann, in attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we will then later on issue these two requests to the two offices I mentioned before, and we may now start with the witnesses Mr. Fila is calling today. I wonder whether the registry --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. When you indicated that you had put in the request, you were referring to Mr. McFadden and the doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought you were talking about requesting for these witnesses authorisation from New York to testify, and we have already done that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I wonder whether the registry -- may I have the first witness brought in? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hereby solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, I hope you feel comfortable. This is your second time here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a debutante, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, on the 10th of June, '98, give a statement to my investigator, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you see if this is the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D149; English translation, D149A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If no one has anything against it, I hope that you will accept this as Exhibit number 149D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Was it signed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you repeat, have you recognised this signature? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I declare that I have recognised my own signature, and the text is based on the statement I gave to Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you would tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Prosecution has any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not seen this previously, so this is the first time we were looking at it. If we could have a moment just to go through it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, you may start.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you have known Slavko Dokmanovic since when and how well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I have known Slavko Dokmanovic since mid 80's. I believe I know him rather well because our acquaintance has been growing firmer until a few years ago over the whole period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one period since 1991, you have together been ministers in the government of, what's his name, the Serbian district?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In '91, we have been together in the cabinet of the Serbian government of Baranja, and Western Srem. I was Minister of Education and Dokmanovic was Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he like to cooperate with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, as Minister of Agriculture, worked for better conditions of living in the circumstances he was in. We did not behave as ministers. We behaved as public persons. We worked for harvesting. We worked for the well-being of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he elected to the government? How did he come about -- how did it come about that he was a minister? How was he elected to the Serbian district? Please always wait ten seconds before your answer. How did it come that Slavko Dokmanovic was elected minister in that government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: All of us were elected ministers. All of us were elected ministers, I was saying, based on the proposal of people from our local communities, that is, municipalities, on a higher level, speaking in terms of the hierarchy of the former Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of man was Slavko Dokmanovic and why was he proposed to that post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was a very well-renowned man in his area on the territory of the municipality of Vukovar, on the entire territory of the Vukovar Bosnian Baranja region, Osijek region. He has, for many years, been active in sports organisations, more specifically, soccer organisations, and that's where I know him from because I took part in the same activities in the sports organisations and the soccer club. He was known as a generous man in his environment. He cared very much for sports ethics and morals. I visited with him frequently, and I know this well, and you should be aware of the fact that a countryside like Trpinja is getting more urbanised, and construction is going on widely. He was head of department, head of many -- Mayor and, as such, overlooked construction activities. Slavko Dokmanovic was generous, sincere, honourable, free man, a courageous man who, in those difficult times when we saw our state fall about, found himself in the service of people who maintained that it was best to keep things as they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he in the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: He was president of the assembly, of the municipal assembly of Vukovar, but the mass media sometimes called him Mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then on the 19th of November, '91, there was a session of government in Erdut. On the following day, was a decision made that you should meet in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Goran Hadzic, who then acted as president of the government of the Serbian region of Vukovar, Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem invited all of us present to meet in Vukovar on the 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go because those were still difficult times, and one took a great risk travelling in all directions because from Baranja, I had to cross the territory of then SFRY, passing barricades, et cetera, so I only followed those summons which I couldn't avoid. I considered that particular invitation to be formal and I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later, that government that you served on ceased to exist, and a new government of the republic of Srpska Krajina was established. Were you a minister in that government too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was Minister of Education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Slavko Dokmanovic on that government too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic was not on the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina because at that time, I don't know very well myself, I don't know why he wasn't, but I later, making inquiries, found out that Mr. Dokmanovic did not have the quality to meet the basic criteria that had to be met for appointments to the government of Srpska Krajina; and that criterion was nationalism. While Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic had beliefs which were met with a certain protest in wider masses of the people, because he did not act, in their view, as an honourable, courageous Serb, that he must, in their view, have held other beliefs. And he was, as such, not qualified to act as a minister of that government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was left out because he was a bad minister, but because somebody thought he was a bad Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I'm sorry. I have to agree with your opinion. I must say that Mr. Dokmanovic, in the belief of many, really many, and they were 282, he was not a good Serb and he did not meet their requirements of that environment, because he was a compromising man. He was not convenient at that time. He did not meet their interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it come about that he became president of the municipal assembly in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, we saw certain political changes on the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, because somewhere in March or April, UNPROFOR arrived to Yugoslavia. In 1994 and '95, UNPROFOR has already played its role and then UNTAES arrives. Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was, by then, used up and rejected. And then with another change in the political current, things that Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic had believed in throughout come to the forefront, and Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was, at that time, politically dead and resigned. But at that time, with the change of the political current, he was simply, again, proposed, elected, and forced to take part in the political life, at one point, as a deputy to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take part in negotiations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: He was forever a loser. He did all the hard work, and whenever it was award-winning time, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic tended to be forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the negotiations in Erdut, was he reputed as an uncompromising, hardline Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Dokmanovic was known at negotiations in Erdut as a moderate, a very moderated man, indeed. I can maintain this with every conviction because I called him in a friendly manner many times at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why was he removed from the post of Mayor in '96?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Why? Well, listen, I should say that radicals awoke again, and because he was not a radical, he was removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he criticised in Borovo newspapers for his participation in the peace making process?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, he was. He was criticised not only in the newspapers, but also on the local radio, television. He was reviled in personal attacks of individual people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you say he was a bad Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was criticised as a bad Serb and because his reactions and his opinions seemed to indicate that he would like to see Serbia again in the hands of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were interrogated before on account of Mr. Dokmanovic. But I would like to ask now, why did he invite you to come with him and what was the purpose of his trip?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, there is inside us something that can be seen in the eyes, and I was on rather good terms with Mr. Dokmanovic for over 15 years, and our eyes said that we are facing a moment of truth. And the truth was that Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic believed those who said that we were going to Vukovar for the purpose of selling Serbian property in the region. He invited me and served me those same untruths, to the effect that we were going to serve Serbian interests in Barinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Because we have the same mindset. I do what I say I will do. I keep my word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is, did Mr. Dokmanovic invite you to save your own property or to save everybody's property?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Everybody's property, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one last question, over 1991, including that session of the government in Erdut and later, do you recollect what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic appeared, as all of us, in various combinations of clothing. Most of all, he appeared in a multi-coloured hunting jacket with trousers, but he also wore civilian clothing, because you must understand, you must remember, that we were poor at that time. Hardly anyone wore suits and ties. It was a matter of our customs and ethics. We acted as everybody did. People wore soldiers' uniforms, whatever they could lay their hands on, and we dressed as our financial -- as we could afford.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean to say, did he dress as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I know that for certain. He was a simple soldier. He did not belong to any army unit, not even in peace making, not even in piece time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I beg to tender this as evidence. I have no other comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, did you ever see Mr. Dokmanovic in a JNA reservist uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever know of him to travel around with uniformed people who were guarding him or working with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, nor had I seen it, because Mr. Dokmanovic travelled alone. He did not have any escort or bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm really speaking of the period after the conclusion of the war in Vukovar, so after November of 1991. You didn't see anything then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to concentrate, but I fail to understand your question. I saw Mr. Dokmanovic but he was not surrounded with armed and uniformed people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough, not that you saw, at least?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I used to see him but not surrounded under armed escort. We saw each other at sessions, at least a couple of times each month, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Again, in the period following the fall of Vukovar, did you ever know of Mr. Dokmanovic to visit JNA prison facilities in Serbia, in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that, nor had we ever discussed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that he certainly didn't have the view of an uncompromising, hardline Serb. Just so that we can get that clear, what would you consider to be an uncompromising, hardline Serb? Can you tell us what a person would be, the sort of views a person would hold if he could be fitted with that description, so far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if we analyse such a person, I could give you certain characteristics of persons who could fit into that category, and I have met a couple of them. First of all, it's the category of people who were in favour of a genocide against the Croatian population in the Serbian region and of their expulsion. Secondly, these are the people who looted, burned the property, and so on. Thirdly, these are the people who refused to obey the dictates of the ethics and who refused to obey the dictates of the government that was being set up in this area; and also, fourth, those people who tried to reject all the efforts of the international community designed to reduce the tensions and to introduce law and order and civilisation in the area; fifth, all those people who simply tried to act violently, who never shave, who look slovenly, people who drink a lot of alcohol, who are unreasonable. I can give you some other criteria, but these are the basic criteria -- these are the people who talk about the greater Serbia, and Serbia can only be as big as it is; those people who refuse any kind of discussion, negotiations; those people who act arbitrarily. And Mr. Dokmanovic did not meet those criteria. These were not the criteria that he used in assessing the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, by that, that Mr. Dokmanovic would be the sort of person who would welcome the intervention of the United Nations in this very troubled region of the world?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: All of us welcomed the intervention of the United Nations, but I don't know what you mean, the intervention. When we're talking about the military intervention, that is not something that we welcomed, but the political intervention, the pressures and the negotiations, this is something that we all welcomed. And Mr. Dokmanovic was one of the leaders of this kind of political attitudes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he always have this view or was this something that he subsequently developed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a proverb which says that only a stupid man never changes his opinion. In the 90's when the euphoria of one nationalism began, it caused the second euphoria of another nation, and we really had it good in Yugoslavia. In 1990 and 1991, I was also exposed to pressures and to threats, and I was simply put in a very specific situation. For instance, a Croatian policeman killed my dog in my own house. It was a well-trained Rottweiler. I don't have to tell you what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand what you mean by that, but I think that you said in your evidence that Mr. Dokmanovic was, more or less, considered a bad Serb because he didn't hold strong views and, in fact, he favoured living together with the Croatian people; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dokmanovic did not have anything against the Croatian people. In his own home, Mr. Dokmanovic even had a Croat veterinarian. He died of a heart attack after the arrest of Mr. Dokmanovic. He lived in his house, in Mr. Dokmanovic's house, quite normally. He associated with Croats. We all did. We were -- we used to be best men at each other's weddings, at birthdays, and so on, a lot of celebrations. He was a member of the group who was sad because of this breakup. There were Croats who shared our views. Unfortunately, we were in the minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he advocating that the Croats and the Serbs should live together prior to the war in Vukovar, that is, prior to August, September, October, November of 1991? Was Mr. Dokmanovic advocating that then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely he advocated this idea. This idea was something that was not in favour of the Croat nationalists who threatened him physically. That was the reason why he was disqualified because he was advocating this option of unity, co-existence. Mr. Mercep and his cohort wanted to physically eliminate him, I think, since May, since the events in Borovo. As far as I can remember, Mr. Dokmanovic did not go to Vukovar at all because he did not dare, afraid of his physical safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the medium by which he conveyed his moderate views, I take it that included the radio, television, and the newspapers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he often appear on the radio and television, from what you can remember, at that time? I'm talking about mid 1991, July of 1991; did you ever speak him on radio or television at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I could not give you a specific answer. It was a long time ago and conditions were very bad at that time. And power cuts often happened, and local TV and radio stations were not in existence at that time in July. They appeared later. We had only some hand radio systems, and some people were able to receive that and some weren't. Later on, with the aid of UNPROFOR and the international community, the local media developed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you if I said to you that there is a record being taken down of a radio broadcast from Belgrade through the Belgrade Tanjug agency where Mr. Dokmanovic spoke of the arrival of the Blue Helmets which, I think you'll agree with me, means the United Nations, in Yugoslavia as being unacceptable; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I can't remember that radio programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, I would like to be able to see what is being discussed. This piece of evidence has not been tendered. If it exists, let him show it here. I don't know what you're talking about. If you have a copy, please provide me with a copy, and then you can talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have a copy for Your Honours and a copy for Mr. Dokmanovic. The information I have is in the English language, though, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked 213.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether that will help you very much, Mr. Knezevic. It's in the English language, but it's a report that's written of a radio broadcast in 30th July, 1991. It doesn't matter, though, if you can't, because I will just take you through what is said here and see whether or not you say that's consistent with what --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. You do not allow newspaper articles to be tendered. I don't know who said that, when this was written. I would like Mr. Niemann to bring the tape of the broadcast so that we can hear it. When I tendered newspaper articles about Mr. Berkovic's statements after the trial, that's not okay, but now I have some kind of report. I don't know who made this.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In July, UNPROFOR was not discussed at all. UNPROFOR began to be discussed in December and January.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And please have a look at the title. It says that the Belgrade Mayor rejects the proposal of the U.N. Blue Helmets' arrival. I don't know if Mr. Dokmanovic has become the Mayor of Belgrade, whether Mr. Niemann upgraded him to that title. I can't accept this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can you please clarify the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm questioning the witness on the document, Your Honour. The evidence that has been led in chief relates to a number of articles -- the witness said that he recalls Mr. Dokmanovic espousing moderate views on the medium of radio and television, if I recall his evidence in chief correctly, and that he obviously also spoke to him himself. This is a document which purports to be a record of a radio broadcast from Belgrade. I'm merely putting it to the witness to ask him whether or not it's consistent with his understanding of what Mr. Dokmanovic was doing at the relevant time, Your Honours. I haven't sought to tender it as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila called for it, and I gave it to him, but at no stage have I sought to tender it, Your Honour. I'm merely questioning the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You're simply making reference to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't ask for this to be shown to the witness. The question was whether he heard about a programme. I don't know if that programme exists at all. This is completely irrelevant. This document is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, it's not irrelevant. I mean, I understand the Prosecution is asking the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is okay, but this is not okay. The document is not okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I mean, you asked for this document. Mr. Niemann was going, I think, to summarise the news reported in this foreign broadcast information service report to see whether the witness was aware that allegedly Tanjug, the agency, the news agency Tanjug from Belgrade, issued such a report. So don't overemphasise the importance of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question that Mr. Niemann posed contained a statement whether the witness would be surprised if he heard whether this statement was given on the radio. You cannot tell this from this piece of paper. Let the tape be brought into court, and then I will allow this. The question was not whether the witness has heard a broadcast. This is an admissible question, that's a legitimate question. But Mr. Niemann claims, states that this broadcast existed, that the Belgrade mayor was against the arrival of the blue helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I made no such claim at all, Your Honour, and I resent being misrepresented by Mr. Fila in this way. I am merely asking the witness whether he's aware of it and I am merely asking the witness to comment on it. Now, he's free to do and say what he likes, and at no stage have I sought to continue it as yet, and I would further add that I am somewhat surprised that Mr. Fila is talking about what he will allow into evidence and what he won't. It's not a matter for Mr. Fila as to what goes into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. Yes, Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Knezevic, did you ever hear a radio broadcast where Mr. Dokmanovic was interviewed and he expressed a view that in their final decision -- it's their final decision not to live any longer either in the Republic of Croatia or together with Croats? Did you ever hear him express a view like that over the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard such views being expressed either in the media or in our private conversations, and let me continue in the answer to your question regarding this broadcast. In July 1991, in the territory of Serbian district of Slovonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, we did not know about UNPROFOR and the blue helmets. So this is impossible. Only in November, December, and January we started to discuss officially the arrival of the blue helmets and the Vance Plan. This is too early. The United Nations still treat the whole situation rather indifferently at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is you didn't hear this. You're not in a position, however, to deny that this actually took place, this broadcast, or that Mr. Dokmanovic said these matters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I already said I haven't heard any such thing, and I don't believe it's possible, because at that time, such a term, "blue helmets," did not even exist. We never knew at that time that blue helmets were going to be associated with the UNPROFOR and the United Nations. Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic never spoke about that, not even in our closed circle of friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never heard of any proposal by the European -- the EC monitors, that a peacekeeping force should be deployed in the area? You never heard anything about that as early as July?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. Later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the EC never proposed that a peacekeeping force should be operational in the area in July, or is it just that you didn't hear it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I simply didn't hear that. Perhaps as a result of power cuts which I referred to earlier. I was constantly travelling cross-country, listening to the radio in small transistors, but in July, I had never heard of that, because in July, in our Baranja, there was no war. The SFRY still existed as a State.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Might the document be marked for identification, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Only for identification purposes, P213.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is only for identification purposes. We can keep it, but not as evidence, as an exhibit. Mr. Fila, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask two minor questions? You may clarify, first of all, a question put by Mr. Fila to you and, actually, your answer more than -- the question, according to the transcript, Mr. Fila put to you was: "Did Mr. Dokmanovic dress as a reserve officer?" And I see that you replied: "Dokmanovic was a simple soldier." Now, could you please clarify what you mean by saying that Dokmanovic was a simple soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic, as all citizens of the SFRY, in view of his duties, was compelled to serve in the army. All psychologically and physically sane and healthy men served in the army. Everybody in different units. He was not a reservist officer and he never had a rank. I, for instance, graduated from a reservist officer school, and I have the rank of JNA officer. Mr. Dokmanovic was a simple soldier. I don't know whether in the infantry or the navy or elsewhere. I don't know. But as for uniforms, I say again, there is a difference in the uniform of a soldier from that of an officer, the quality of material, et cetera; and as for Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic's dress, we even joked about his hunting uniform because he was then -- we teased him then, "You are a President and you have the better dress," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep insisting on my question, but when you say he was a simple soldier, did you mean to say that he was a simple soldier in the Territorial Defence or as a reservist? You were a JNA officer, as a reservist, I think, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Whereas Mr. Dokmanovic, unlike you, was a simple soldier, not an officer, but again as a reservist. This is what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain that we all belonged, in a way, to the army, but in the post of Minister of Agriculture, Education, you cannot be an army man at the same time. Mr. Dokmanovic could not have belonged to any army unit of the JNA. On the territory, everything was under JNA control, even the organisation of civilian life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have been told by quite a few witnesses that in addition to the army, the JNA, there was a Territorial Defence and there were reservists --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So what, therefore, did Mr. Dokmanovic belong? To the reservists or to the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: As a healthy man, he belonged, as we all did, to one of three army formations: the navy -- JNA, police, and the Territorial Defence. In that sense, we all belonged to the Territorial Defence. We were on the records as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then this is a different question. I understand that you were Minister of Education serving on the same government as Mr. Dokmanovic. Now, in this capacity, what clothes did you used to wear in that particular period, between, say, September '91 and January or February '92? Did you used to wear civilian clothes or, instead, military clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That depended on the purpose and tasks to be achieved on the specific day. For instance, if I was on the territory of Baranja, I dressed simply so as not to stand out in the masses. I never wore a suit and tie. But if I went in the direction of Vukovar or further, towards the municipality of Erdut, which came next along the way, I wore a so-called camouflage uniform. I believe we all know that they could be bought in shops. I mean, the overalls, because they were very comfortable, you could sleep in them, and then they eased passage through the checkpoints held by the army; we were more easily identified and recognised. We passed more easily and reached our destination more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, therefore, depending upon the area, the territory where you were going and/or where you found yourself or depending upon the tasks you were performing, you used to wear either civilian clothes or military uniform; and in the area of Vukovar and Erdut, you tended to put on a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: For which particular purposes? Just so that you could go through checkpoints more easily?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the first purpose was to overcome the obstacles more quickly, and then we had to go for two or three days with power cuts. We had to sleep in the car very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether there are any questions arising out of my own questions? No? Is there any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much for coming and giving evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, as you know, normally we take a break around 11.00. Do you think it is better for us to rise now and reconvene in 20 minutes so that we don't interrupt their evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you please, Your Honour. Just an apology to you and the Prosecutor. I did not pick up the statements from the following three witnesses. I thought it made no sense. It was a family relationship. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You don't need to apologise. It's quite obvious that there was no point in submitting a statement because they are going to report about his character, personality, and so on. But again, do you think it is better, because I think it is better for us to stop now, and so we reconvene in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to stand and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Dokmanovic, Mr. Dokmanovic is your husband?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have two children?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And two grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another grandchild on the way?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not easy for me also to be asking you these questions, but this is necessary. Could you please describe how you two met, how you got married?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we practically know each other since we were seven. Slavko and I are of the same age and we were born in the same village where we lived. We went together to the first grade of primary school, since we were seven, and we were throughout, the eighth year primary school. After that, we went on to Vukovar, to high school. I went to the higher economic school and he went to the Lise (phoen). Then we went on to Osijek for university studies, I of economy and he of agriculture. In the second year of high school, we started dating, and we married in '69.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do your children do?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Our children are adults. They have their own families and their own children. Our son and daughter graduated from high school and work in the customs [translation interrupted] --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You all live together?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do. We now live in Sombor in a rented house since 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and Mr. Dokmanovic, you are refugees? You have the status of refugees?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe, what is he like as a husband? Did you have any problems with him during your long life together?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We have been married for 29 years, we married young, and I can say that I have had a very good marriage, a wonderful husband, a good father, a true family man for whom the family was always first and foremost, above everything else. He always tried to spend as much time as he could with us. We are always together with our grandchildren, with our friends, either in our own house or in the friends' house. He has always had a big heart. He has always liked to help people whenever he could. For instance, he always lent a hand to people in the same profession. I am an economist and my husband is in agriculture, and people often ask him to lend a hand. Trpinja is an area where people are mostly engaged in agriculture. He has always been willing to help. Whenever people started harvesting or sowing, he lent them assistance with ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your friends, were they exclusively Serbs, or did you also have friends among other ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, the lists of them were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, during this trial, it has cropped up, your relationship with the family Vodicka?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, gladly, although it is very difficult for me to speak about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to collect yourself. This is not easy for any of us here.

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Well, we have known one another since the '70s. I met Jovanka in '72, on the second birthday of our daughter, because she then married Zlatko and came from Sarajevo to Trpinja. Both of them are veterinarian doctors. They got jobs in Trpinja. Zlatko is a Croatian and Jovanka is a Serbian from Herzegovina. Zlatko, since he was on a fellowship of the veterinarian station in Vukovar, after graduating from the university and his army service, his first job was in Trpinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To avoid any problems, please tell me, Mr. Vodicka was a Croat but his mother was a German and his mother a Czech (sic). How was he a Croat then? What did you want to say by saying that he was a Croat? Did he claim that he was a Croat? Was he a Catholic?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He declared himself as a Croat. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. And as I said, his first job was in Trpinja as a veterinarian, and his duty was to go to call on houses and treat cattle, and that's how he came to our house. Zlatko and my husband made friends. At that time, Zlatko was still not married. He often came to us for supper, for lunch, and we made friends. I believe it was in '71 when he first came, and since '72, he has been with Jovanka. We were good friends and our children were inseparable. Our children are of the same age. The went to the same school. Later they moved to Vukovar, and we remained in Trpinja, in our house, but we kept regularly seeing each other almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these events that we are discussing here came -- did Zlatko Vodicka come and where did he come from in October?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He came in the month of October and one -- it was one evening. He came with Slavko. He said he had come out of Ilok, looked for Slavko, and together with him he came to our house, and he remained with us for three weeks until the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's when he left?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He, until recently, worked in Trpinja before the war for about 20 years, and somewhere in the village, he heard on the radio that Mitnica was liberated and that people from Mitnica would be evacuated, I don't know where, some to Zagreb, some to other parts, and since his wife remained at home, he went to look for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mitnica was a part of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of the veterinarian station and the graveyard. He went to look for her. He did indeed find her. They came to our place together and stayed for four or five nights, and then they moved to our neighbours' because we were overcrowded. Our daughter with her baby was with us. There were a lot of people coming and going. As I said, we were overcrowded, and to keep us comfortable, they moved to our neighbours' where they spent some time until they redid their own apartment in the spring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vodicka has died in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He died on the 15th of September, 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was after the arrest?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was after the arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have friends of other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, a lot of them, actually. In fact, none of us were really interested in nationalities. Vukovar has always been a multi-national, multi-ethnic environment, and nobody really cared for other people's nationalities. We were friends and acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it important for your husband, nationality?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't matter at all to Slavko, and Zlatko would not have otherwise dared to look for him and stay with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Dokmanovic, throughout all those years you spent together, since you started dating --

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-nine years of marriage plus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- has your husband ever been convicted of anything? Was he fighting? Involved in any fights? Was he expressing national hatred?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: "No" to all those questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will repeat because we do not have your answers. In Trpinja, was there water and electricity in Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, because -- I can't tell you the exact date but sometime since August 1991 to the spring of '92, because networks were broken, cables were down, and works couldn't be executed at that time. Not everyone in the area got electricity back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army in this period managed to provide a power generator, so from time to time you did have water?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Trpinja is a village which is not plugged onto the network of Vukovar. We had our own water supply and our own water well and we had a pump supplying that water. It was an electrical pump, so during the power cuts, we were deprived of water as well, and people needed water to wash, to feed the cattle. As I said, we are an agricultural area. There were households which at that time had over a hundred pigs, for instance, and we couldn't carry water from God knows where. So we had our own water supply in cattle sheds. From time to time, we got supplied with water in the morning and filled the reservoirs, buckets, whatever. Sometimes it lasted for an hour, a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Slavko dressed in this period, November?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: In November, you say? Slavko was usually dressed in hunting clothes because civilian clothing was difficult to launder and iron, especially suits, whereas hunting dress was easy to launder. We just hung it out to dry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you now to have a look at Defence Exhibit 48. Is that the clothes that you're talking about? D48. Is that something that you submitted to me as clothes that he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is it. That is the jacket -- the vest, sorry. Yes, this is the shirt and the trousers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is -- what shall I call it? -- a jacket or -- a warm jacket. He had this as an agronomer. This is actually working clothes he received to work in in the field, during the harvest, during the sowing season, and in cold weather, they used to wear these fur-lined jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are the clothes which he was wearing during the incriminated times?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He wore this in cold weather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what you gave to me?

utterances.speaker: DANILKA DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This concludes my examination. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I assume there is no objection to the witness being released. Mrs. Dokmanovic, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, are you going to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I have two more witnesses, and I should conclude with them. We work until 1.00; is that correct, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Until 12.30, and then we resume at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. All right. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, what is your relationship to Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He is my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the year of your birth?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th December '73.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Higher agricultural school in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I ask you a question, please make a ten minutes' (sic) break before you answer?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished high school for agriculture in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ten seconds, not ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ten seconds, I'm sorry. I said minutes, didn't I? Ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then, will you tell us, when did you serve in the army? When did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from high school in 1991. I spent my schooling in Vukovar, and I served the army in Raska. On the 18th of December, I started my national service, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Raska, that's in the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go back from the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: '92, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go back on that date?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in our unit, as with any other unit in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, came an order that all the soldiers from the former Yugoslav republics should finish doing their national service in the place of their residence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Vukovar was your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Trpinja, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? You went back to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I finished serving the national service in Vukovar. Then in 1996, I got married. That was in March. I have a son, eight months old. Unfortunately, my father hasn't seen his grandchild. Right now, I live in Sombor, in a rented house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Vukovar in 1996, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the transitional customs service. That was an UNTAES body. And when I went to Sombor, I continued to work in the customs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father opposed to you working for UNTAES?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of his tenure as the president of the municipal assembly in Vukovar, did he have anything against the presence of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he took part in the negotiations concerning the Erdut agreement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any problems because of that caused by extremist Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was threatened, intimidated. They said that he was not good enough as a Serb, and he was attacked because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean, "a good Serb" ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My father was never a nationalist and that's why he had problems. He was a moderate man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the circle of your acquaintances, your family, your father's friends and your friends, were there people of other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Our best friend was a Croat; unfortunately, he's dead. I think it says enough about what kind of a man my father was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In conclusion, please tell us: As a father, was he a real parent to you or whether he tortured you, whether he was a drunkard, a violent man, and all the worst things you can say about a father?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My father is an honourable and an honest man. He is a good parent. He always advised us how to deal with problems facing us in our lives. He never beat us. All the problems that we encountered, we solved by talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You live together; you all live together with the exception of your father, unfortunately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's your sister, your brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: My wife, my son, my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your sister is about to give birth?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in mid July. That's why she's not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, that's why she's not here?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness, I imagine there's no objection to his being released. Thank you so much for coming to give evidence, Mr. Dokmanovic. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, what is your relationship to Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko is my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live and what do you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I live in the village of Trpinja, the municipality of Vukovar. I work in agriculture. I'm self-employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spent all your life in Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born there; I went to school there; I married there; and I live in our old family house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is that house from the house where Slavko Dokmanovic lived?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Up to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's practically one in the same farm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not the same farm. It's the same street. The houses are 500 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your common property?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. His house is his property, and the family house is both of our property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a deserted house?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I live in my own house. Slavko's house is deserted. I house-sit for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much is it worth, according to today's prices?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 100.000 Deutschemark, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do Serbs sell their property now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He wouldn't receive more than 50, according to the real estate agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of man has your brother been?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
