utterances.text: We spent a lot of time together in the same house because I was -- I have been motherless since a very small age. His wife and he took care of me. My brother saw me through school until I got married and started to work myself, until I was 25 or 26.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean your brother Slavko?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Slavko took care of me. He went to parents meetings for me when I was in school. He saw me through school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a popular man in Trpinja and how popular was he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He has always been popular since a young man, a soccer player, then as a good agronomer. People often came to our house while we still lived together to solicit advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he popular only with Serbs or other ethnicities as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: People of other nationalities lived in the village too. He had very good friends among them. And his best friend was a Croat; he was almost a member of the family. His name was Zlatko Vodicka, the late Zlatko Vodicka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you react when hearing that Slavko Dokmanovic was arrested for such a crime?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: At first, I was shocked, and then I felt some sort of revolt. People were taken aback, asked themselves why; how on earth? They were mostly taken aback.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at these documents, please, and tell us what you gave us when you came here?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D150.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us what this is all about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a petition written by the population of the village of Trpinja. There are other people signed here as well from the surrounding villages, some sort of protest or solidarity with their ex-citizen, to the effect that they disagree with his arrest because he has not deserved this by any of his actions; a statement to the effect that they want to justify his role in the village as an honourable man, an honourable citizen, hard-working man who has helped a great deal the entire village in its main activity and also in sports activities, et cetera; and to help prove his innocence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our system, this is accepted as evidence. If your system does not accept this as evidence, please admit this as an exhibit -- please have it marked for identification, I mean, what his wider community thinks of him. If you can, if you possibly can, admit it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If we might have a moment. Your Honour, the only objection we would have in regard to this is just that there's no verification of reliability. I mean, there appears to be a number of signatures on here, but there's no way of knowing the authenticity of signatures or names or anything at this point. And that would be our objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see your point. On the other hand, this is evidence relating to the character of Mr. Dokmanovic. And, in addition, as you know, the court has the power to decide upon the probative value of each document. So although it is true that there's no authentication of the signatures, I don't see why we should not admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. That's our --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm sorry, Mr. Williamson, for interrupting you, I have an original which I will hand to you. These are original signatures here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The question is not -- of course you will admit into evidence the original. The question is not that we were not given the original, but the question is that there is no authentication of the various signatures. However, in spite of that, if the Prosecution has no major objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's our only objection, Your Honour. If Your Honours are prepared to admit it then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Counsel, please take this original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 150, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, another thing, throughout this period, you said you spent your entire life in Trpinja. Will you describe war events in 1991? Were any bombs thrown on Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war which began in '91, sometime in June, July, there were exchanges of fire over barricades. There were bombs falling on Trpinja and surrounding villages, shells also, grenades, mortar fire. There have been casualties. And shelling came from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Territorial Defence involved in the village of Trpinja?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I, as every other man who served in the former JNA, and I was issued a uniform as some sort of reservist. All other men did the same. All healthy men under the age of 60 had to belong to some sort of reservist formation or the Territorial Defence, according to the constitution of the SFRY. Thus, all of us men in the village had to do the same thing during the war. It was not even in the village. It was duty on the street, some sort of outlook posts, lookouts. We kept duty service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any fighting outside the village?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we remained in the village. My duties were on my own street, on the crossroads, and on the entrance from the side, from the direction of the village of Dalj. That's where we spent all this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the situation with electricity and water supply during wartime, November, December?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe power cuts began at the end of July. We had more problems being deprived of water than being deprived of electricity. We suffered from lack of water until we got a water pump, an electrical water pump, which worked for about an hour or two every day. The village suffered, although many houses have their own wells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you dress at that time? Specifically, how did Slavko Dokmanovic dress?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We had to dress according to the situation. We had to wear clothes which were easy to launder, clothes which could do without laundering for several days running.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brother served in the army as everyone else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he served, what was he; an officer, a general?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a simple soldier. His national service was in Krusevac. It was an ABH service. He did not receive any rank, then or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a uniform ever, an officer's uniform, active or reservist officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. Except, perhaps, during military actions, we soldiers put on those uniforms we were issued, but that was rare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was only in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was only inside the village. Those were old and hardly usable uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, you yourself put on the uniform sometimes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as we were ordered, according -- following military orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning that Slavko, too, sometimes put on that uniform in the village?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be good for you to describe that uniform.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: We called that the drab, olive colour, thick cloth, especially in cold weather. We wore overcoats, mostly to protect ourselves from the cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williamson? Cross-examined by Mr. Williamson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, you indicated that in Trpinja, there was some shelling and exchanges of fire over barricades in June and July of 1991. There was very little damage, though, in Trpinja; was there not?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say when the shelling took place. There was some damage in Trpinja, but since the village itself -- that's the life in the village. When a shell fell on a house, then the same day or the next day, we would fix that house immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in comparison to what happened to the Croatian areas in Vukovar municipality, Trpinja came out pretty light, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, if you look at it that way, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released? Thank you for coming to give evidence in court. You may now be released, Mr. Dokmanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my next witness is due to appear at two. That's the expert witness, and that's my last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So this afternoon, first of all, we will hear your witness, Professor Aleksic. And then I understand the investigator, Dzuro for the Prosecution afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Only two witnesses this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And then we would have our two additional witnesses ready tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning. So tomorrow, again, only two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So that means that probably tomorrow we can finish by lunch time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think they will be -- I think it's foreseeable that we could finish by lunch time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I was rightly reminded that tomorrow morning at 9.30, we have the initial appearance of a new indictee, of an indictee who has recently been arrested and brought here. This will be held at 9.30. I propose, therefore, that we reconvene at 10.15. And then, of course, if we need some time, we could continue in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If that's the last one, somebody asked me to stand in for him tomorrow morning. So I will be here tomorrow morning if that's the one. I don't know if that's the one. So it won't take long because I won't be defending him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's just an initial appearance, but I will be happy to see you already at 9.30. Good, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. May I ask the witness to be so kind as to make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise because the Prosecutor has received only a draft of this document, but I wanted to provide as long an expert opinion as possible so that I can ask as few questions as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, are you a professor? Were you born in 1931 in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the Belgrade law faculty?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an assistant lecturer and then a lecturer?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lecture abroad, in the U.S., in Japan China, U.S.S.R.?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I was a visiting professor in several countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You published, as far as I can see, lots of books?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm also quite old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you publish more books or do you have more years?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have more years than I have published books. It would be good if it were the other way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can see that you were the President of the Yugoslav Society for Criminal Sociological Research?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the Association of Lawyers in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the editor of the Law Review?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Archive for the Legal and Social Studies?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You trained police forces in international organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zambia, Sweden, Germany?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also an associate -- you also cooperated with the United Nations with regard to drug problems?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spent several years as a President of the Association of Teachers of Law as part of the Association of International Law for Peace?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you are also a member of this council of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a representative of Yugoslavia in the Association for International Law?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please check whether this is your CV, and if it is, I would like this to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D151 and the English translation D151A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that there are no objections for this document to be admitted as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at those documents and tell us whether this is your expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D152 and the draft English translation D152A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A part of the penal code of SFRY was translated later due to lack of time, and I would like this to be appended to the previous document. So this is not to be admitted as a separate Defence Exhibit, this is just a translation of a legal text. If there are no objections, I would like to tender the expert opinion as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no objection, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This last document will be marked D152A/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, it is usual before this Trial Chamber, when an expert is -- it is usual for an expert of your profile to be questioned when the sentencing is about to begin?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what happened in the Tadic case -- well, we have changed the rules somewhat -- and you are being questioned before the Trial Chamber brings its decision whether the accused is guilty or not. It is therefore important to note now, what did you use as a basis for your expert opinion? What did I give you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I received from you the amended indictment, and I used it as a basis for the consideration and comparison with the former penal code in SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which law was in force from the 28th of September of 1976 onwards and, please, just continue?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I express my respect to the Trial Chamber and all the others who will be listening to me. I want to say that the penal code of SFRY was passed in 1976, but it came into force only in July 1977. It was in force for the entire territory of SFRY. There were several amendments to the law, but those amendments did not apply to Chapter 16, which is the topic of our discussion here. The amendments were elsewhere. The situation lasted until 1990. In 1990, the Official Gazette of the SFRY, on the 6th of July, 1990, published the amendments of this very chapter, Chapter 16; and in the articles contained in the amendments, it introduced several new elements, and also the punishment of the confiscation of property was repealed. These amendments were provided to you, were published in the Official Gazette in 1990, and they mostly refer to a certain expansion of the criminal offences, and there are some new articles; for instance, you will see in the law, there are some articles designated A and B. For instance, Article 150A, 150B, it concerns repatriation and so forth. You have to understand this because most criminal offences in the SFRY were punished very strictly after the war. That's the period from 1945 until 1950, right at the beginning in the fervour of deliberation and the fight against fascism. Of course, there were many executions that were not strictly legal and decisions which are not legal and which we copied the U.S.S.R. practice. By 1950, things calmed down a bit, and from that time onwards, we had the usual situation. A number of perpetrators of criminal acts died, simply died, those who were not discovered, and this act was not something that happened very often. I would now like you to go to the end of my expert opinion. For your purposes, I studied the information, the data, from 1980 until 1990. Of course, I was surprised myself because that period, from 1980 until 1990, had very few cases, and, in fact, the same situation applied from 1977 when this law came into force. We had about two or three convictions a year. You can see that there are some death sentences but you also have sentences of three to five, five to ten, ten to fifteen years' imprisonment which obviously indicate that this is a case of aiding and abetting. According to the report published by the Yugoslav Statistics Office, I even found a suspended sentence. I did not have enough time to study that particular sentence, but it is absolutely true that since 1987 until 1990, there were no convictions for criminal offences described in Chapter 16. It's like some kind of a calm before the tempest that struck my country, what was then my country and what is my country now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 1990, the First Amendment was passed in 1993. That's in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What changed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The first Official Gazette of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that's issue 35/92, after that there were certain amendments, and then there was the 16th of July, 1993, where it was published that death penalty, the capital sentence, is abolished in the penal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it was furthermore added that the sentence of 20 years' imprisonment was prescribed for the most serious offences. So in 1993, 20 years of imprisonment was the prescribed sentence. Up until that time, 15 years of imprisonment was a maximum penalty or the death penalty which could then be reversed or commuted to 20 years. So it was considered that 15 years' imprisonment was the most severe sentence unless the death penalty was commuted to 20 years. After 1993, the death penalty was no more, only 20 years' imprisonment, and confiscation was also abolished as a sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, if you look at the indictment, you know what you have to say. Can you please tell us, what about the forms of aiding and abetting or being an accomplice?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The issue of being an accomplice in the penal code -- I know that you're all experts in law, so you know that it's a very serious question. It's a difficult question for students when they have their exams and later on in courts, the judges have many problems when they try to determine the truth. The penal code of SFRY recognises different forms of being an accomplice. The most serious one is when a person is a co-perpetrator. I don't know whether I should define what does it mean if one is a co-perpetrator. I will just tell you that in Yugoslavia, both in theory and practice, that the theory of distribution of roles was accepted so that the co-perpetrator is a person who acts together with other persons to perpetrate the criminal offence and the commission of the act is their joint objective. So this is the theory with which you are all very familiar. I have to say that Yugoslavia, and Serbia in particular, had a penal code as early as in the 14th century, but later on, when Yugoslavia came into being after the First World War, we were under the strong influence of the Roman law, I mean Italian and French law, and later on German and Austrian law, so this is what we had to build on. At any rate, any perpetrator is responsible within the limits of his mens rea, so if you have two persons who perpetrated the criminal offence, if one person expands his intention, so if they attack a woman wanting to rob her and then one of them rapes her, the person who raped her is responsible singly because that was not their joint intention, that was not what they wanted. Incitement is also very strictly punished in our country because we deem that a person who incites another person to commit a criminal offence has to be punished as if he had committed the crime himself. I think this is a general fundament which is present in most of the penal codes today. So incitement is when you incite the person who has not formed the intent to commit the criminal act, and by inciting him, you actually aid him to commit a certain criminal offence. Of course, you can also incite a person who has already planned the commission of the act but has not made the decision to actually execute the plan. So if the person who incites another person, who has already formed the plan, the intention to commit the crime, then this is not incitement but so-called failed incitement. As for aiding, which is also a form of being an accomplice, I would like to pay some more attention to that since I can see that this is charged in the indictment. First of all, I have to say that I am not familiar with this element. If I'm not mistaken, it says there that a person -- that he aided and abetted. We do not have this in the Yugoslav penal code. We have the aiding element, but this other element, I have to say, with all due respect, that it's very dangerous to introduce those elements into the penal code which allow the judges a lot of leeway in interpretation. It is punishable in our penal code if somebody, with intent, aids another person. Such a person will be punished as if he had committed the act, and the sentence can be commuted. As regards aiding, the spectrum is very broad. It contains advice and all forms of encouragement to the perpetrator. However, in the old Yugoslav penal code, we insisted on the intent to aid the perpetrator, and the act had to be perpetrated. What does it mean, the intent? It means that the decision is made and that that person is mentally responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't be aiding somebody by chance?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. There has to be an intent. It may be, for instance, guarding in front of the door or it can also be, for instance, you take somebody for a walk knowing that the burglar will commit a burglary during that time and so on. Aiding presupposes that a person has already made the decision to commit the criminal act, and that corresponds to the nature of the relationship between the perpetrator and the aider, the abettor. The abettor has to have the intent. It is impossible to have the aiding and abetting without the intent. So you have to have the awareness. It is possible to punish, with a less severe sentence, the abettor, especially in relationship to the co-perpetrator and the person who incited somebody to commit the crime because this is a less severe form of being an accomplice, and also it makes it possible for the abettor to change his mind and to make it easier for that person to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the practice of Yugoslavia? Were abettors punished as severely as perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: They were punished much less severely, and in Chapter 16, which is under consideration by the esteemed court, as you have seen in this list -- it is a brief list but I can't invent more cases than there actually were -- you can see a difference every year between severe punishments of perpetrators and more lenient sentences to aiders, aiders and abettors, because an abettor can be a political -- can be a person who has the same political views or espouse, et cetera. Anyway, the court does not punish them with equal harshness. Also, the limits of criminal culpability are clearly defined, and if you look at Chapter 25, I am prepared to give the court our penal code from that time, and I also have a doctoral thesis of a current professor from Kragujevac entitled "Aiding as a Form of Complicity." We also have a very serious form, and that is the forming of criminal associations deserving very harsh sentences under our code, but this concept presupposes the existence of a plan, and every action outside that plan is something of individual culpability. One of the other things which I noticed in this indictment and which would have been treated differently in Yugoslavia, better or worse it is not upon me to say, but following European traditions, we treat the acquiring of criminal acts as they are treated in Europe. In this law of 1770 -- 77, it says that if the perpetrator committed several acts for which the perpetrator is being tried simultaneously, he will be given a joint sentence for all of them. The joint sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just to correct the transcript. Here your words were translated as follows: "... we treat the acquiring of criminal acts as they are treated in Europe." Probably you meant -- of course, I'm sure that your language was quite accurate -- probably it should be "concurrence."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Concurrence. "Concurrence," not "the acquiring."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You all know that very frequently -- thank you for this intervention -- you know that very frequently in life, we have before the courts perpetrators and delinquents who do their crimes in various manners, and the court treats them differently. I will say more about that later. But according to the indictment, the Yugoslav penal code, and I believe European penal codes, we don't have this characteristic that one act can involve four or five different criminal acts. If I stab somebody and then break his rib and then stab him through the heart, it is one murder. I cannot answer for it by being charged on four or five counts. And as you know, we were under Turkish occupation for very long, and one of our public figures Vaso Peligic (phoen), was sentenced to 101 years, and all for writing one book because this book did have this effect and then it had this effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, for interrupting you, but what matters is Chapter 16, which we are discussing here. Chapter 16 envisages certain criminal acts which you omitted to mention but they also contain other crimes, murder, et cetera. Are they treated in the same way in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Criminal acts from Chapter 16 exist in accordance with Chapter 141 in accordance with the capital crime of genocide. I must say one thing about the entire Chapter 16. Yugoslavia, the SFRY, as most countries, both in Europe and America, Asia and so on, has signed conventions which obligate our country to execute these conventions in their own legislations, and the provisions of these conventions are translated into the provisions of our law, and these laws repeat word for word what is said in the conventions. However, there are certain conventions which deal with particular subjects, like the conventions we've had since 1990. For instance, postponing the repatriation of captives. If somebody killed this prisoner, he cannot answer for both murder and for postponement of repatriation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about, for instance, genocide. Genocide is murder. According to the practice of our courts, would the person guilty of genocide be also answerable for murder, heavy bodily injuries, et cetera? What is the essence?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We widely practice the method of consummation, which means that if a person commits a crime, in order to reach the highest point of the criminal ledger, he commits a number of crimes along the way. We, in punishing him, take into account the last, the most serious, the gravest crime. Our theory boils down to the belief that adding up various charges would make no sense, so we use consummation. I could point out a number of examples from various conferences because anything up over a certain number of years looks more like revenge. A person is heavily punished, even with 40 days of gaol, not to speak of years and decades. We tried to lengthen our sentences, prison sentences, but there was a wide protest. Those are eternal discussions of criminal law, and if we turned to the past, we would find many examples of the same. If someone, in committing a crime, deserved a prison sentence, his sentences may be put together, but not over 15 years. I hope I was clear. So we have, for instance, a number of crimes, and we add up the sentences, but the sum turns out to be over 30 years. In this case, we have to take a maximum of 15 years. That is the main point of our law. This is sometimes misunderstood by the public. The law also contains an instruction. If, for instance, our clause 4 of article 48 prescribes prison sentences of four years, then the joint sentence cannot exceed eight years. If we take fines, we have the same principle working. We envisage only one fine for multiple violations. So this is an ideal example of concurrence. We stand firmly in our law on the standpoint that there is an ideal concurrence of crimes, not of criminal laws. If this principle is based, as it is in our case, on a realistic view which is based on the real circumstances of the real world, then one act can have implications in several criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation is not very good because the matter is complicated, so you must try to be slower.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm used to be listened to by students and I don't often take care of this. You see, there is also the apparent concurrence when an act corresponds to several descriptions of a criminal act but only one, in fact, is applicable. Then this apparent concurrence may be ideal or real. I have to apologise to the Trial Chamber. I know that you are very well familiar with this, but I'm now in a situation where I have to tell you what the solutions were in the former law. From the extended criminal act, there is -- it boils down to one criminal act. Let me tell you just one more thing: In the theory of criminal law, there are several cases of apparent concurrence. There are three groups. The first group is made up of cases where apparent concurrence arises from the relationship of persons involved. And the second group contains cases which relate to the subsummation of one criminal act into another on the basis of the specific instance. The third group is the legal unity of various criminal acts. I will now tell you something about the extended, protracted criminal offence. As far back as in 1965 in December, there was a convention of the Supreme Court of Yugoslavia. And although this is not the law and we do not have the proceedings, the opinion brought at that convention is still valid in the practice before our courts. For the extended or protected criminal offence to be in existence, it is necessary for one person to commit two or more offences of the same kind but of separate nature, each of which contains all the legal elements required for that very same criminal offence, either the more serious or the mitigated form. There has to be a certain continuum in time linking all those offences. All the charged offences, from the standpoint of a reasonable view, can be viewed as a unified whole. The construct of the protracted criminal offence is used very often in Europe, and it is not in contravention with the requests of the criminal policy that are valid right now. For the conditions of this offence to be met, it is not important that a person is a perpetrator, a person who insights or aids or abets the criminal offences that are a part of the protracted criminal offence, may be committed by acts, omissions, or may also be attempted criminal offences. What is interesting for this Trial Chamber is that in combined cases, the legal qualification for these kinds of offences is always done in accordance with the most serious legal qualification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean that if somebody is an instigator or an abettor, he is always treated as a perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Also the identity is taken into account, the nature of the culpability and also the manner in which the criminal offence was committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, just one clarification --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I just have the sentencing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have enough time. Let me just clarify one thing. With the criminal offence of murder, we have homicide, murder, cruel murder, murder out of a vendetta, and so forth. If somebody commits one of those crimes, is he tried for only one aspect of the crime or is he charged with all the aspects?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, murder is a horrible event in the life of any man or the society as a whole, but there are different kinds of homicide. First of all, for instance, you have the mitigated form when a child is killed during the birth or you have the violent and cruel murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if somebody commits a cruel murder -- so first it is a murder, and then it is a violent or cruel one -- in SFRY, did we try somebody for murder and for cruel murder or just for one of them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, just for one of them and the more serious one. There is a special kind of homicide in the penal code of the SFRY. That's grievous bodily harm which is compounded with death. So we now look at the intent of the person who committed the murder. If it's a manslaughter, then it's a manslaughter. If there's intent present, then it's homicide with intent. But if somebody hit somebody else, and that other person fell down and died right at the spot or later in the hospital, then we go to the intent and we use the qualified form of the grievous bodily harm. So that's grievous bodily harm qualified by death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So death was not something for which intent existed?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To conclude, I tried to make it as fast as possible. That's the issue of the fundamentals. You gave us the schedule of sentences until 1990. And let us repeat chapter 16, these are criminal offences against humanity and international law?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's chapter 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was valid in 1990 throughout the territory of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, it was amended?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, it was amended, in fact. So in the provisions of the penal code of SFRY, it contains provisions how the sentencing is to be carried out. Can you please explain to the court: When the court gave out the sentence, what factors did it take into account, taking into account, of course, whether a person was a perpetrator, an instigator, an aider, an abettor. What else in addition to that was taken as mitigating circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The penal code envisages certain sentences, certain forms of punishment, but these are never given as categorical. There are always alternatives. There is always the range between this sentence and another sentence because that's life. And all the judges in the world want to individualise the sanction, the penalty, what is the right measure for that man. After all, even when you take medication, the dosage is not the same for each man. You have to take into account specific circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's go on to the provisions of article 42; what are the mitigating circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Fila is actually taking his revenge. He used to be my student and now I have to listen to him. There was a congress in Argentina and then in Paris in '71. All these elements were taken into account. And today, in fact, the extreme cases are no longer applicable; although, for instance, in Greenland, they have some very strange sentences. Our penal code uses the criminal responsibility as the basis for the sentence, for the punishment. Secondly, we apply the principle of individualisation. Thirdly, there is the unity of objective and subjective circumstances, and none is given priority. It is up to the court to decide. And, finally, the criminal law in our country deems that sentencing is up to the judges. It is a judicial function. And judges use the results of the scientific research and of expert opinions of other people, knowledge of sociology, psychology, criminology, and so forth, but they have to stick to these provisions. Article 48 sanctions the sentencing; and in articles 42 and 43, it provides for mitigating circumstances. The general rules for sentencing are as follows: Degree of criminal responsibility; the motives of the criminal act; the seriousness of threats or injury to the protected property; circumstances in which the crime was committed; previous life history of the perpetrator, taking into account the fact that some people may get derailed from their goals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, so that's the previous life of the person who committed the crime?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's right. Then personal circumstances. And one thing we pay a lot of attention to, and that's the conduct after the commission of the act, of the criminal act; and other things that speak to the personality of the perpetrator. So these are the circumstances which I can now elaborate, if you want us to. But I will thank you for your attention, and I want to save myself from my former student.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask one more thing. The passage of time from the commission of the act until the trial, is that taken into account as well?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I referred to it as the conduct of the perpetrator after the commission of the criminal act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a long time has passed, so if the perpetrator was not caught in the act, if a long time has passed, in accordance with our law, was the conduct of the perpetrator taken into account in the sense of whether he continued committing criminal offences or whether he acted within the law, whether he kept himself within the law?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Our law, the penal law of SFRY, also has the statute of limitations. There are people who are not tried if the statute of limitations expires. But if the law gives him that possibility, it obviously envisages that such a person has not committed any other criminal acts in the meantime. And, of course, the conduct is looked into very carefully. There are some people who are at liberty because there wasn't enough evidence to convict them. You can take that into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the health state of the person also one of the elements taken into account?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the health state, also at the time of the commission and later on, is taken into account. In our penal code, like in other penal codes, we have provisions indicating that if a person, after conviction in sentencing, is diagnosed with a certain illness, we can have a review of the case to see whether the decision was right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not referring now only to mental illnesses but also to physical illnesses. Is it also a mitigating circumstance?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Of course, there are cases where the responsibility is excluded due to those cases. In Yugoslavia, physical conditions are taken into account more than mental, but I'm of a view that certain mental conditions can affect the development of a person, and the sentence should strive to bring him back into the fold. And if we're dealing with a younger person, the sentence should not put him in a situation where he will just be remembering his criminal offence and where he will think of it as a bad dream and where he can continue to live normally. It would be, indeed, horrible if everybody who came under the influence of the legal machinery, if those people were marked. Just like in the former times, people were branded with the letter "L" or "T" or thief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In conclusion, the purpose of punishment in Yugoslavia was rehabilitation and not revenge?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, this should be so in any civilised country. I have to tell you, you are young, my colleague, Fila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would not say so.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You are younger than I am. There are people who are even younger than that. I, unfortunately, lived in the era which was under the strong influence of Oshinski (phoen). In the Yugoslav criminal law, the Prosecutor's office was deemed to be the right hand of the court, and the Defence counsel should cooperate with the court and should tell the court what the perpetrator has told him in confidence. Those were the trials where a person walked in and then was executed right away. I was horrified by that. In my country, the situation was better than in Russia, but it was horrible all the same. From that time on, with the permission of Mr. Prosecutor, I always tell my students that in the 21st century, they should succeed in achieving that the Prosecutor's office should not be in the same building as the court is. The Prosecutor's office has to have the strong apparatus that would be used to help him, but when they appear before the court, they should be just one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're now referring to our domestic courts, not the Tribunal, but we have been through something that you are lucky you haven't been through, so we always have to take that into account. I think that Winston Churchill said that "Communism was good for us but not for the Englishmen." Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Fila. Prosecution? Cross-examined by Mr. Niemann:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We meet again, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I hope with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you were saying in your evidence, a moment ago, about what we call cumulative charging, that is, where one person is charged with a number of offences rising out of a set series of conduct, and you were discussing the instance of murder and cruel murder. What would happen in the former Yugoslavia in a situation where a person was charged only with cruel murder, that being the most serious offence, and the court came to the conclusion that the accused was not guilty of the cruel murder but had, in fact, committed murder? Would the person be acquitted?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are opening a subject which is very complex, that is, the identity of indictment and the verdict. In our country, it looks usually like this: If the Prosecutor does not react in good time and if he doesn't change the qualification, he risks losing all together. But in such matters when charges are similar, the judge is entitled to change the qualification during the trial and Prosecutors usually look upon it as their own credit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen in a situation? What do you consider the situation would be if there was no power for the court to change it, if the court had no authority to change it from, say, cruel murder to murder once it had seen the facts?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Theoretically speaking, if that provision did not exist, then the court would refuse the indictment, and that would be in bad taste, unusual, irresponsible. But if we were to support the theory of absolute identity of charges, then all such people, due to the fault of the Prosecutor, would remain unpunished, because the court would then not have the right to be flexible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, Professor, that if you had a situation where neither the court could change the indictment to reflect the actual crime itself, and it did find that a murder had been committed, and the person was acquitted because it couldn't change the indictment, that there could be no subsequent trial for murder because the person would have been through a trial and would have been acquitted. So the acquittal would stand against any further Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean, but I believe it would be unrealistic to think about a situation where it would be permitted, that due to differences between indictment and verdict, something like this could happen. But still I'm under the impression that you agree with me. Sometimes I surprise my students by stating that the truth is not the main principle in trial proceedings. I certainly won't surprise you. However, if we take non bis in idem, we can't try one person for the same thing twice, and if the judge does not object, one cannot be sentenced to a harsher sentence than asked for. And there are a number of things which support the rights of the defendant. However, I believe the court has a certain authority to be flexible, to be flexible and, on the other hand, the Prosecutor's office lives in the same house as the court. I believe in your system, in Rotterdam, for instance, there is subordination. The Appeal Court can issue orders to a lower level court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Professor, I think in your extensive studies overseas, you would agree with me that in some jurisdictions, this problem is resolved by the Prosecution filing an indictment which contains cumulative charges, and the court can then deal with the issue on sentencing in terms of what is the appropriate penalty to be applied. So the emphasis is not -- the critical point is not the conviction stage, but the sentencing stage. Do you agree with me, that you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, with all due respect for you and my pleasure at knowing you, don't mind my saying that in a lawyer's jargon, it is called shooting with a shotgun. If we take it that there are enemies 1, 2, 3, and under item 7, we write all others for whom there is grounds for suspicion, I don't think your formulation is very happy (sic). If a doctor, for instance, examines a patient, he carries out cumulative laboratory and other analysis but he treats one disease.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really wasn't asking you whether it was a process or system with which you agreed. I merely was asking you whether it was one with which you were familiar?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that you would tell me that in Europe, in the civil systems, the approach is not to charge cumulatively, but to give the judge the power to impose or find the appropriate crime to fit the facts, should that arise; if not in your jurisdiction, certainly in other jurisdictions on the European continent?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did I -- was it the translation? You said "civilian proceedings."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I called it "civil proceedings," and I really am referring to proceedings other than those known as the common law.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We, in Europe, differentiate between principles working for the civil proceedings and the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I think the Prosecutor was referring to civil law systems, what you called before criminal systems of Roman-Germanic origin, say Yugoslavia, Germany, France, Italy, and so on, as opposed to common law systems. So it has nothing to do with civilian proceedings.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We call that continental law. Mr. President, I do not know of a single criminal proceedings in Europe where it would be allowed to use a shotgun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I wasn't asking that, but I'm not going to go into the virtues of duck hunting.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, that is an area widely lied in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, in your paper that you have kindly provided us with, you deal with the law of the SFRY and then its amendments under the code of the Federal Republic in 1993. I think you will agree with me, the law of the FRY, SFRY, certainly would apply to what is now the Independent Sovereign State of Croatia but the law of the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, has no application to that country.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Certainly, but as far as I know -- you know, I've been a law professor in Croatia for a long time, an honorary professor, and I have very nice memories of that. They took over the SFRY law for the first period, and since 1992, they've had their own provisions of their own making. You may correct me if I'm wrong. But at the time of the event you are discussing, practically nolens volens, the same provisions applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's probably quite right. The question that I'm asking you, though, is really, when you make reference to the FRY amendments in 1993, am I right in saying that they only apply to the member states of that federation and not to Croatia? And my next question is: Do you know what amendments were made to the law of Croatia after 1991? Do you know whether that was amended and in what respect, or was it similar to the amendments that were made in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I must say that amendments to the Croatian law followed the conventions signed by the SFRY because they were common to all countries; and as for the SFRY, their own amendments abolished the death sentence earlier than we did. We abolished it in 1993 and they abolished it in 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we are looking for guidance as to sentencing practices for an offence that was committed on the territory of Croatia, it's true, isn't it, that we would look to the law initially of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and then, ultimately, to any amendments that were made to the criminal law of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a proviso that I would ask you to look at amendments from 1990 made in the SFRY because they were specially dedicated to Article 16 and they added to the criminal acts, expanded on them. You have postponement of repatriation among these changes and other charges which were not earlier written in Article 16, Chapter 16. I suppose that that coincided with what happened in 1990 in Croatia, it was a renaissance of provisions or a modernisation of provisions originating in 1990 -- 1992 because provisions from 1977 followed the convention signed by Yugoslavia and which Yugoslavia had to incorporate in Chapter 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, quite so, Professor, and I think we're all grateful to be provided with Chapter 16. The point I am making, though, is relevant to the question of sentencing, and the law of the SFRY is not very helpful to us, I think you would agree, because it deals with the minimum sentence of five years and then the death penalty which, of course, has no application in this jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I would not be that categorical. For instance, Chapter 16 begins with Article 141 envisaging a sentence for genocide, five years or death sentence or, 142, war crimes against civilian population, five years or death sentence. You delete the death sentence because it was later substituted by 20 years. War crimes against casualties or prisoners, five-year sentence or death sentence. Crimes against war prisoners, it says: Will be punished by at least one year. Then organising a group, ten years. Illegal murder of prisoners of the other side, ten years. Use of illegal unlawful means of fighting, at least one year, maximum 15 years --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can see entirely, Professor, that there are penalties, but the point I was trying to make was that --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to help you with your earlier question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm grateful, Professor. Professor, you touched on momentarily the issue of intent under the law of the former Yugoslavia, and if I understood what you said previously, that under the criminal code of the former Yugoslavia, you didn't have premeditation as such. You had two levels of intent, one was intent and the other was possible criminal intent, which was a species of negligence.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I must correct myself if I was imprecise. For a criminal act in the SFRY and now, premeditation and guilt have to be components, and culpability has two components: intent and negligence, whereas sanity has always to be present, complete or reduced or moral insanity, whichever. So there is always intent and negligence when we speak about a criminal act. I don't think it is different in any other country. A whole series of Italian criminal law experts supported the theory that intent has to exist. We, in the SFRY, did not have the concept of premeditation. Some other countries have it. I don't know whether it is good or bad, but we do not have premeditation as a concept. Perhaps it is a useful gradation of intent, but we don't have it. We just have intent and negligence. There are, however, qualifications, such as possible intent. For instance, a person driving a car without brakes and with shaven tyres, and the person drives slowly thinking he can manage to drive his aunt to the railway station without any accident; however, the accident happens. But that is the possible intent. So even intent and negligence have their gradation. You have conscious and unconscious intent or negligence. You have a woman working in the lab and handling, without enough care, explosive gas which causes an accident. If an unqualified person, such as a char lady, handles things in the lab and causes the same thing, her guilty, her culpability would be different. She is unqualified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I said to you, Professor, that in some jurisdictions, negligence cannot be the basis of criminal liability?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I would like to live in such a jurisdiction. But, you know, we have murder out of negligence. You have a person sitting in a train. A heavy suitcase from the opposite side falls on the head of a child sitting underneath and the child dies. I don't think that the person would be saved from criminal charges even under such a jurisdiction. For instance, you answer for murder for injuring peace of Queen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Queen's peace, I believe the doctor wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Or, as somebody said, it doesn't matter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we lost the Professor. I am honestly sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you provided us with some statistical information in your report relating from the period 1980 to 1990, and I think these were offences under Chapter 16, prosecutions for offences under Chapter 16. Do you know what gave rise to these cases? Were these World War II cases, or what was the background to them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: For some of the cases I know, especially since Mr. Fila and his office dealt with some of those cases, there are very complex matters involved and there are also foolish cases. I know of a case where a person came to Bosnia and asked the municipality to issue him with a certificate that he was in an SS division during the war so that he could obtain a pension in Germany. Of course, he was detained in Belgrade and convicted to 10, 15 years. So that even judges asked him, "How on earth did you think of such a stupid thing to do?" However, there were also cases where people thought that the Statute of Limitations expired and there were comparisons of photographs involved. In one case, I was asked as a forensic expert to define by an ear whether this man was the one who cut people's throats. For instance, also the Sakic person who is being delivered to Croatia, some people simply wanted to go back and die in their own homeland. Then there were also cases when criminals were caught when they came to their parents' funerals or to sell their houses; anecdotal cases, in fact, where the less serious sentences concerned cases with families, lovers, et cetera. I wanted to take cases from 1977 to 1990, but there were no such cases until '88. In '78, there were only two cases of this kind. From '87 to '90, I did not find a single case that would fit the description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be fair if I was to say that most of the cases that would have been the subject of your cumulative table here, from 1980 to 1987, were cases which arose out of the events of World War II? It doesn't matter where, but during the course of World War II?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: They were very old. Take that into account. Forty plus years since the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to do any study or carry out any analysis of any cases that may have arisen as a consequence of this most recent conflict from 1991 onwards? Have you seen any prosecutions for war crimes or genocide in relation to those events?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: There have been a few cases of prosecution, and I had the pleasure of leading a project titled "Women in the War." It is a very moving book. You must understand, Mr. Prosecutor, that Serbs are studying those cases which were against them, as the other side studied crimes against that side. The project I am talking about involves 80 women raped by mostly Muslims but also Croats. Women's names are not mentioned, only code names are used. At the promotion of the book, the women spoke of very moving details, stories about rape being used as a ticket out, and all the 80 women attended the promotion. A couple of them reconciled themselves to all the consequences, they told us their real names, and they stood up and said, "Yes, I was raped. I would have done anything to save my child which slept nearby. I stood up and kissed their hands."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, yes, what I was mainly interested in was cases which had gone through the process and there had been a conviction and the penalty had been imposed. Do you know of any cases like that since 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have some of those cases. We have a very strange case in Croatia -- I didn't manage to get the file. I hope it will be sent to me by my ex-students from Croatia once things calm down. It involves the murder of ten to twelve soldiers on the bridge in Korana near Karlovac. The perpetrator was arrested and tried, but it was established that he was not guilty by reason of insanity. Things were very bad for some time but are beginning to improve. If you know the configuration of Bosnia where a lot of those things happened, there are places very high up in the mountains with holes, deep holes, and in cases of murder, victims were often thrown into those holes. Later on, heaps of bones were extracted from those holes. Victims of Croat forces were found, victims of various other divisions, victims of crimes of passion. I personally believe it is not okay that these holes were cemented in former Yugoslavia. It is almost as if the former regime was afraid that its own executions would be later discovered. I don't know if I have answered your question. But if you wish, I can try to find in Serbia what you looked for --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I was merely asking you about recent cases. We'll move on. Now, you talked about this concept of co-perpetrators, aiding and abetting and so forth. I think you're probably aware that the Tribunal's Statute and Rules of Procedure has its own regime to deal with that as well. It doesn't need to depend upon the law of Yugoslavia. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm aware from the Statute of your court, which I esteem very highly and wish it success. You said in one place in the Statute that the court has to familiarise itself with the law of the country from which the Defendant originates, and I said I believe that was right. If you agreed to borrow our concept of cumulative sentence, I don't know, but we do not have any other concept and I don't believe anything else is applied in Europe either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you a question about that. I want to posit to you a situation and ask you if you could tell me how a court in the former Yugoslavia would deal in its sentence with a situation such as what I'm about to give you. It's an example. Say you have an offence committed by a large corporation, a company, and the managing director and members of the board --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt. A company in Yugoslavia cannot commit a criminal act. We do not provide for criminal responsibility of legal persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Professor. We'll get there. The managing director and the members of the board agree that they wanted to commit a fraud, and they use the lowly company accountant to actually carry out the mechanics of the commission of the fraud. If it came to sentencing, who would receive the greater sentence: the managing director and members of the board, or would it be the accountant?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, during the trial, we would have to establish the identity of the perpetrator and his intent, and then we would have to establish who he was instigated by, who he was enabled by, and who aided and abetted him. We often meet situations in our practice where the director enters a liaison with a deputy chief accountant. He provides her with the papers, she uses those papers to actually get disbursements of money, and he is often -- in such cases, it is often difficult to differentiate between the perpetrator and the abettor. The director cannot be responsible for everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So would it be fair to say that -- assuming you can prove the board and managing director actually agreed that this crime would be committed and then directed the accountant to commit it, you would agree with me that the board and managing director would be the most culpable criminally, wouldn't you? That would be the normal position?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The one who allows him to act in this way and whose knowledge is involved would be the most guilty, but a whole number of people would be guilty. This category of economic crimes, white collar crimes, are very widespread now. In such cases, perpetrators, the real perpetrators, protect themselves very well, and it is usually the small fry who gets sentenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, one last question: Does the Statute of Limitations apply to Chapter 16 offences?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wish to assist so I don't have any questions. If it would be of interest to the court to establish the forms of culpability, intent, premeditation, and so forth, the Professor has it right here in the introduction to the penal code and he can read it, and it says quite clearly there what is negligence, what is premeditation, what is intent. He can read it. It's very short. If, of course, the court is interested in it. That would be the answer to a number of the questions posed by my esteemed colleague, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, I don't think it's particularly relevant to the court, more so because we, under our own Statute and the customary international law and international criminal law, we have to proceed on the basis of international law notions. In addition, I have realised that Professor Aleksic is as familiar as I am with a masterpiece, Jescheck, what I consider a masterpiece in criminal law, and I'm sure also Mr. Waespi is familiar with that, in addition to Mr. Fila who actually mentioned Jescheck in one of his briefs, so we know all the basic notions prevailing in the best legal literature in continental Europe. We should now take a break, but I have three questions. I wonder whether you would like -- if I can ask you these three questions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer today or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. The question was not tomorrow. Right away or after the break in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you seem to be an ally of my wife. You want to have me back home as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, probably it's better to rise now for 20 minutes and then we go on with our questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. May I be excused after the break? I have another matter in another court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Professor Aleksic, I have, actually, three questions. First of all, I understand that previously, prior to 1993, most crimes provided for in Chapter 16 carried a sentence which could go from five years in prison to 20 years or death penalty. So I want to understand the rationale behind this choice, maximum of 20 years or, as an alternative, the death penalty. So no provision was made for, say, an imprisonment of 25 years or 30 years or life imprisonment and so on. What was the rationale behind this lack of -- and provisioned this particular point?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the system of criminal sanctions in the law of the SFRY ranged from very low, very light sentences for, I think, six months in prison up to 15 years. I think that was the law in SFRY. In exceptional circumstances with very serious criminal offences, in addition to the 15 years imprisonment, there was the death penalty which was equal to 15 years imprisonment. But since our legislator's never directed the judges to issue sentences but allowed them to apply mitigating and aggravating circumstances, even in this most serious sentence, the legislators provided the alternative, death penalty or 20 years. So the sentence of 20 years imprisonment does not exist, according to that law. We are now talking about the period from 1993 forward. In 1993, the death penalty was abolished and the 20 years imprisonment sentence remained. But I have to tell you once again, Mr. Fila has more practice than myself, so he probably knows more about it than me, but the sentence was never 16, 17 or 18 years. It was either 15 or 20 years. So 15 and 20 years, there was a vacuum in between those two sentences. So the maximum sentence was 15 years imprisonment, and the minimum would be three months and maybe even less. And when the death penalty was given, it could be commuted so the 20 years imprisonment was the commuted sentence, because there was some ray of hope that the convict could be rehabilitated. In 1993, the death penalty was abolished and the 20 years imprisonment remained automatically, but it was not the range up to 20 years. It was up to 15 years and then there was this 20 years imprisonment. I don't know if I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, probably I didn't make myself clear, because I was wondering why the maximum imprisonment is 20 years and why there's no -- is there any reason why or a particular reason why before '93, as I say, for the most horrendous crimes, say, somebody killing 50 people, an uncommon crime, without any relation with war or armed conflict; so for this set of crimes, a multiple crime, a murder, you would get either 20 years or a death sentence, whereas in most European countries on continental Europe, you have, say, a maximum life imprisonment or, say, 30 years, 35 years. So why, therefore, is there this gap between -- nothing beyond 20 years or life imprisonment? Actually, I read in the English translation two judgements delivered by a military tribunal in Belgrade in early '93, I think, for war crimes committed by Croats, and there some of them were sentenced to 20 years, some to 15, and one or two to a death sentence, and they were executed. So, again, I'm lost to understand the rationale behind this particular way of providing for sentence, for penalties.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have to defend my Professor Srzentic. He was the legislator involved in creating this law. In the long discussion, private discussions that we held, he told me certain things, and I think they will serve to clarify this point. First of all, we thought that today it is very hard to defend the existence of the death penalty. But due to certain specific factors, we allowed it. I have to tell you that the death penalty was given very rarely. There is a statistical report of the statistical office of Yugoslavia regarding the death penalty. I can provide you with a copy of it. I have it here. They showed very clearly that nolens volens we did not have the death penalty, although there were some cases. In Slovenia, there hadn't been a case of the death penalty for over 40 years; and even in Montenegro, there weren't that many death penalties given. So the legislators took the following stand: The death penalty is something horrible, but at this stage of our development of the criminal system, we have to keep it because our population still has this system of an eye for an eye. Second thing, when the death penalty was to be replaced by the life imprisonment, the associations of penologists in Yugoslavia felt that this was even worse than murder, than killing a person, because it was dying by inches. In particular, the provisions in some other jurisdictions which stated that a person could not apply for parole before 20 years of his life sentence, and even in some cases, there was life sentence without parole. We thought it was horrible so we said that the death penalty should exist, and if it is too harsh a sentence, it should be replaced by 20 years. This is something that makes other people confused because they think that we have the sentence of 20 years imprisonment. We do not have this sentence, in effect. Even those people who examined students in criminal law, when they are in a bad mood, they ask the students, "What's the maximum prison sentence in Yugoslavia?" And if the person says "20 years," he fails the exam. I hope that now you understand what the situation is. But I can give you an explanation for 1993. The death penalty was abolished and 20 years remained. And the new penal code, which is being drafted, there are certain tendencies for 30 years imprisonment and so forth. In Croatia, it is the case already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question relates to what you said about aiding and abetting. I know, of course, that you don't have this notion, which is typical of common law countries. In continental European countries, of course, we have the notion of complicity which is, to some extent, broader. However, talking of aiding, you said that in Yugoslav law intent is required for the aiding to be regarded as a crime. I don't know whether this is a question of translation, whether you really require that the aider should have the intent to commit a crime or a simple knowledge is sufficient. Let me give you an example which is taken from the case law of war crimes tribunals relating to the Second World War. The case of some people, some military officers go into a place with intent of actually arresting or even killing three POW's, prisoners of war. Now, the question arose whether the driver who drove them to that particular place where they shot the three enemy officers, whether the driver was aiding and abetting the crime. And the court said that what was crucial was whether they had the knowledge, whether the driver was aware that he was driving those people to go there and to arrest and possibly shoot them. And if he was not aware, then he was not, in a way, an accomplis. And, actually, one of them was not found guilty because he was not aware at all. In this case, therefore, knowledge is crucial, not criminal intent. The driver had no intention because he was simply unaware of the purpose of that trip to a particular place.
